name: Funding crowding filter on buy-and-hold (BTC, ETH daily)

sections.hypothesis: Holding BTC or ETH but stepping into cash while their perpetual futures funding is crowded (7-day average 30% a year or more) gives a better risk-adjusted return than holding throughout, after costs, because crowded leveraged longs precede liquidation-driven falls.
sections.rationale: Perpetual futures funding is paid between longs and shorts every 8 hours to keep the perp near spot. High funding means the market is full of leveraged longs paying to stay in; a fall can then cascade through forced liquidations. That is information about positioning that isn't in the spot price chart, and every price-only idea in the trial log has failed or turned out to be trend following. Kestrel only reads the data (Binance's public archive, every 8h since 2020-01); it never trades perpetuals, so Australia's limits on retail perps don't apply. Weak points: funding rises in strong bull markets, so stepping aside when it is high may mean missing the best runs (the same way Fear & Greed contrarian sold the start of 2020 and 2024's rallies); funding was much wilder in 2020-21 than since, so the signal may fire mostly in one regime; and the threshold is a judgement. Disclosure: before writing this note I looked at the funding distribution itself (7-day annualised average at or above 30% on 11% of days for BTC and 13.5% for ETH, 2020-25), but not at any returns conditioned on it.
sections.rules: Daily bars. funding_7d = the average of the coin's own perpetual funding settlements in the 7 days up to the bar's close, each rate annualised (rate per interval x settlements per year), each settlement known from its settlement time; unknown (null) when the window starts before the history or the newest settlement is more than 1 day old. Crowded = funding_7d at or above 30% a year, about 3x Binance's default rate of 0.01% per 8h (about 11% a year): a round multiple of the exchange's neutral level, not fitted to returns. An unknown reading leaves the base position unchanged. Decide at the close, trade at the next open; 2% no-trade band; long only, spot; 10 bps fee, 1 bp half-spread, square-root impact. Base position: fully invested. Target weight 0 while crowded, 1 otherwise.
sections.falsification: BTCUSDT 1d and ETHUSDT 1d, 2020-01 to 2025-10 (funding history starts 2020-01; the holdout starts 2025-11), default parameters, 330 USDT, run once each. Reject unless, on both markets: (1) Sharpe is above buy-and-hold's; (2) max drawdown is no worse than buy-and-hold's; (3) total return beats the market held at the strategy's average exposure (the report's 'at the same exposure' line), so the time out is better timed than random; (4) break-even cost is at least twice the cost paid. A pass goes to robustness and walk-forward before any decision, against a deflated Sharpe counting every trial.
sections.parameters: crowded_pct 30. Only this is pre-registered; any other threshold is a new trial.
sections.costs: A switch in and out each time funding crosses 30% a year: perhaps 5-15 round trips a year at about 22 bps each, on a position that is otherwise held. Whipsaw around the threshold is the main cost risk.

history.reason: Pre-registered test (BTCUSDT and ETHUSDT 1d, 2020-01..2025-10, crowded_pct 30; runs 20261113-073754-e1a047 and 20261113-073756-eb5043). BTC passed all four rules, but only just: Sharpe 1.070 vs 1.067 for holding, drawdown -75.3% vs -76.6%, +1,223% vs +1,165% for BTC at the same 89% exposure (holding made +1,420%). ETH failed rules 1-3: Sharpe 0.87 vs 1.12, drawdown -79.3% vs -79.3% (marginally worse), +760% against +2,286% for ETH at the same 87% exposure. Stepping aside on high funding missed more of ETH's rallies than it avoided falls. Another threshold, or BTC alone, would be chosen from these results: a new note and new trials if ever tested.
